opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by just prompting the model as far as it can go. For a new feature, I'll write a system prompt, maybe add a few examples, and get a prototype in front of people quickly. That tells you whether the idea is useful at all, and it shows you where the prompted version breaks: where it misreads intent, gets the tone wrong, or can't handle edge cases.

Those failure modes become the spec for the real work. Once I know what "good" looks like, I write evals first, both automated ones and a set of qualitative examples I check by hand, because otherwise you can't tell whether training is improving anything. Then I think about the data. Sometimes that means synthetic data, where you use the model itself, guided by the prompts that worked, to generate examples of the behavior you want, then filter and refine them. Sometimes it means collecting human demonstrations or preference comparisons.

From there it's very iterative. You train, run the evals, look at the outputs yourself, find new failure modes, adjust the data mix, and repeat. You also have to check that teaching the new behavior didn't regress something else, like making the model more verbose or worse at refusing appropriately.

I think of the prompted prototype as the cheapest way to learn what you're building. Prompting tells you what the model can already almost do, and training turns that into something reliable and robust.

r001.rationale: The response says the prompted prototype reveals where it breaks, and that those failure modes become the spec for development and evaluations.

r002.rationale: It mentions checking for regressions in other behaviors, but does not propose additional evaluations to detect overfitting to the primary evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about it is that the prompted prototype is really a hypothesis about the behavior you want. It's the fastest way to see what the model can do today, and it tells you where the gap is between what you can get with just instructions and what you actually need the product to do.

So the first thing I do is basically live with the prototype. I use it a lot, I give it to other people, and I'm looking for the failure modes. Where does it break? Is it a knowledge problem, a formatting problem, a judgment problem? Those are very different. A lot of the time you discover that the prompt is doing a lot of work to compensate for something the model doesn't natively have, and that's the signal that you need to move beyond prompting.

Then the second step is turning that intuition into evals. I think this is the part people skip, and it's the most important. You take all the examples where the prototype did something wrong, and you write them down as concrete test cases with a clear sense of what good looks like. Sometimes that's a rubric, sometimes it's a reference answer, sometimes it's just pairwise preference. But you want something you can run every time you change anything, because otherwise you're just vibing.

And honestly, that eval set often becomes the spec for the model. When you go to the post-training side and say, "here's the behavior I want," the eval is a much better description than a paragraph of English. It forces you to be precise about edge cases, about tone, about when the model should refuse or ask a clarifying question versus just going ahead.

From there it's iterative. You collect data that targets those failure modes, you train, you look at the evals, but you also go back and use the thing qualitatively, because evals always undercount the weird stuff. And you keep the prompt in the loop too. Sometimes after training, you can delete three quarters of the prompt because the behavior is now in the weights, and that's a really satisfying signal that the model has actually learned it rather than just following instructions.

The last thing I'd say is that you have to resist the temptation to over-specify early. The prototype is there to learn from, not to lock in. If you commit too hard to the exact behavior of your first prompt, you miss the cases where the model's own judgment is better than what you wrote down.

r001.rationale: The response says to identify where the prompted prototype fails and turn those examples into concrete test cases.

r002.rationale: It recommends qualitative checks because evals can miss unusual cases, but does not propose additional evaluations to detect overfitting to the primary evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I usually start with the behavior I want the model to have. Can we get something close just by prompting it? That gives us a concrete prototype to react to, and it helps us figure out what we’re actually asking the model to do.

Then I look at where it breaks. Is it misunderstanding the task? Is it missing context? Are we being unclear about what a good response looks like? I want to distinguish those problems before deciding that we need more training.

From there, it’s an iterative loop: collect examples, build evaluations around the failures we care about, improve the model, and see whether those improvements hold up on new cases. The prompted prototype is useful because it makes the idea tangible, but the goal is to turn that promising behavior into something reliable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to build evaluations around the failures of the prompted prototype, directly linking evaluation design to baseline failures.

r002.rationale: It says to check whether improvements hold up on new cases, describing additional evaluation beyond the cases used to guide development.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the prompted prototype as a way to make the behavior concrete. What do we want the model to do, and what does a good response actually look like? Then I’d collect examples, including cases where the prototype fails, and turn those into an evaluation set.

From there, it’s an iterative process: improve the prompt, identify which limitations persist, and decide whether those call for better data, fine-tuning, or a change to the product itself. I’d keep testing against the original goal, because improving a benchmark isn’t necessarily the same as making the model more useful to someone.

r001.rationale: The response says to collect cases where the prompted prototype fails and turn them into an evaluation set.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes benchmark improvement from usefulness, but does not propose additional evaluations to detect overfitting to the primary evaluations.
